meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'The earth is degenerating, children no longer obey their parents'?
meta.ogDescription: No tablet, no museum, no cuneiform. The oldest version anyone has found is from a 1908 magazine for cyclists — and it said 5000 B.C. and named a different king.

answer.label: Nobody in Assyria — a modern American invention
answer.authorDates: Anonymous · earliest located appearance August 1908, in print
answer.sourceLine: There is no Assyrian tablet. No museum holds it, no excavation report describes it, no Assyriologist has published a translation of it, and no cuneiform text corresponding to it has ever been produced. The oldest version anyone has traced appears in Bassett’s Scrap Book for August 1908 — an American magazine for cyclists — where it is credited not to an Assyrian tablet but to ‘Naram Sin, 5000 B.C.’ The now-standard wording, with the date 2800 B.C. and the words ‘the end of the world is evidently approaching,’ was fixed by George S. Godard, State Librarian of Connecticut, in his annual report of 1922.

source.heading: The source
source.excerpt: Our earth is degenerate in these latter days; there are signs that the world is speedily coming to an end; bribery and corruption are common; children no longer obey their parents; every man wants to write a book, and the end of the world is evidently approaching.
trail: Quote Investigator’s survey of the digitised record puts the earliest known instance in Bassett’s Scrap Book for August 1908, page 84. The text there reads ‘We have fallen upon evil times, the world has waxed old and wicked… Each man wants to make himself conspicuous and write a book’ — and it is credited to Naram Sin at 5000 B.C., supposedly from the Imperial Museum in Constantinople the trail ↗.

Over the following fifteen years the attribution wandered freely: 3800 B.C., then 2800 B.C.; Constantinople, then Istanbul, then unnamed museums; an apocalyptic clause about ‘the end of the age’ appears by 1920. The wandering is the tell. Genuine artefacts do not change date by two millennia and museum by continent from one printing to the next.

The version quoted above — the one now reproduced everywhere — comes from the Report of the State Librarian to the Governor, State of Connecticut, 1922, page 93, where George S. Godard presents it as an Assyrian tablet of 2800 B.C. Every later ‘Assyrian tablet’ citation we have seen descends from this form.

Afterwards it kept travelling: reassigned to Egyptian priests by 1925 and again in 1948, and to Cicero by 2001. A saying that can be handed to a Sumerian king, an Assyrian scribe, an Egyptian priest and a Roman senator without anyone noticing is not a translation of anything.

One internal giveaway is worth naming. ‘Every man wants to write a book’ is a complaint about a print culture with cheap publishing and too many authors. It is a natural thing to say in 1908 and a strange thing to inscribe in wet clay.
source.excerptNote: The 1922 wording, as printed in a US state librarian’s annual report — the moment the floating complaint acquired its permanent costume of ‘Assyrian tablet, 2800 B.C.’ Read it as what it is: an American librarian’s wry aside about too many books, dressed for antiquity.

source.rightsNote: The 1908 magazine item and the 1922 Connecticut state report are both American publications well before 1929 and are in the public domain in the United States; as anonymous or official texts of that age they are equally free in the UK and EU. There is no ancient original whose rights could be at issue, and no translator to hold any, because nothing was translated. Reproduce it freely — but reproduce it with the true date attached, which is the whole point. This is not legal advice.

author.name: Assyrian clay tablet
author.heading: Why it gets pinned on an Assyrian tablet
author.metaLine: c. 2800 BC · a source that does not exist
author.bio: The tablet is the only ‘author’ on this site that has never existed. Assyria is a real civilisation with an enormous surviving literature — tens of thousands of catalogued cuneiform tablets, many in the British Museum, covering law, omens, letters, epic poetry and a great deal of accounting — which is exactly what makes the fake work. Readers know the tablets are real, assume this is one of them, and never ask for a catalogue number. Genuine Assyrian and Babylonian texts do complain, at length, about bad times and worse neighbours. None of them complains that everyone wants to write a book.

misattribution.heading: The attribution problem
misattribution.intro: Most disputed quotations have a real author who has been swapped for a more famous one. This one is stranger: there is no earlier version to recover, because the antiquity is the invention.

items.why: No accession number, no museum, no excavation report, no published cuneiform text. The date 2800 B.C. is also awkward for anyone checking: it sits before the Assyrian empire people picture when they read the word, in a period whose surviving tablets are overwhelmingly administrative the investigation ↗.

The oldest instance found credits a Sumerian-era king — the historical Naram-Sin reigned in the 23rd century B.C., not the 50th — and places the object in Constantinople. Within fifteen years the king had vanished and the tablet had become Assyrian.

items.who: George S. Godard, Connecticut State Librarian
items.why: This is where ‘Assyrian tablet, 2800 B.C.’ is fixed, along with ‘the end of the world is evidently approaching.’ That does not make Godard the fabricator — he was repeating a story already in circulation, and we have no evidence he coined it. It makes his report the ancestor of every later citation.

Reassigned to Egyptian priests in 1925 and 1948, and to Cicero by 2001. The complaint is stable; the civilisation is interchangeable. That is the signature of a floating saying rather than a document.

The ‘children now love luxury, they have bad manners and contempt for authority’ line credited to Socrates is a different fabrication with its own paper trail. People often cite the two together as mutually corroborating. Two unsourced quotations do not corroborate each other.

misattribution.truthLine: No Assyrian original exists. The earliest located version is an American magazine item of August 1908 crediting a different king and a different millennium; the ‘Assyrian tablet, 2800 B.C.’ form dates from 1922 the trail ↗.

context.heading: Why it resonates
lead: It is the most comforting fake in circulation. Every generation suspects the young are worse and the world is ending, and this hands you a 4,800-year-old scribe saying the same thing, which means the panic is old, therefore wrong, therefore you can relax. That is a genuinely useful thought — it just did not come from Assyria.

There is a cost to the shortcut. The line is usually deployed against people who are worrying about something real, and it works by borrowing authority it does not have. The honest version of the argument survives without the prop: complaints about generational decline are extremely well documented across recorded history, and you can cite the documented ones.
context.detailsSummary: How the story mutated, decade by decade
detailsBody: 1908: Bassett’s Scrap Book prints it as Naram Sin, 5000 B.C., held in Constantinople. No apocalypse clause yet — just evil times, corrupt politics and too many authors.
1908–1913: the date slides to 3800 B.C. and then towards 2800 B.C. as it is reprinted.
1920: the first version that ends with the world approaching its end.
1922: George S. Godard’s Connecticut state library report fixes the canonical text and the ‘Assyrian tablet, 2800 B.C.’ label.
1925 and 1948: reassigned to Egyptian priests. 2001: reassigned to Cicero. Still no tablet.
context.pull: Every man wants to write a book. Said the ancient scribe, in clay, apparently.
